messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The assault happened on a Tuesday in late October, right at 4:30 p.m., while Sione was tightening the busbars on a new service panel in the back of a downtown community center. He remembered the moment not as a flowing sequence but as a series of sharp photographs: the heavy steel door slamming shut behind him, the blur of two men stepping into the work light, and the sudden grip on his shoulders. When his partner later asked how it had unfolded, Sione found he could only point to those frozen frames. He felt certain that large gaps remained in his account, as though the missing film had been cut from the reel entirely. The sudden pressure of their hands had left him braced against touch, and any unexpected movement nearby still drew a quick, defensive reaction from him. He held the event against his own character, certain it happened to him simply because of the sort of man he was, and someone with sharper instincts or a heavier build would not have ended up pinned against that panel. Afterward, the late afternoon hour became a threshold. Every day at 4:30, the light in his truck would shift, and a quiet detachment would settle over him, making the steering wheel and dashboard feel distant and unreal. He began steering clear of unfamiliar clinics, warehouses, and even new job sites, unable to trust his ability to read the threat in unfamiliar spaces. At work, the habits compounded. Sione spent long hours scrolling through games and social feeds, letting the screen hum drown out the echo of the slam. He paired the quiet hours with a daily ritual of two beers and a prescribed muscle relaxer, keeping the quiet steady. He avoided television and news segments that lingered on street violence, preferring to keep his attention fixed on familiar routines. The avoidance carved a quiet distance into his relationship with his partner, Maya. When she reached out to adjust his collar or tap his arm, he flinched before he could catch himself, retreating into his phone rather than meeting her eyes. His refusal to take on the site supervisor role felt less like a career pause and more like a narrowing of his world. The guilt arrived with the memories. Whenever the late sun hit the window at 4:30, or a heavy door echoed down the street, Sione would feel a sharp, familiar weight in his chest. He blamed his own character for the event, convinced that his quiet nature had made him an easy target, and that the guilt was his due. Over the months, the hopelessness settled in like a low tide. He watched his days repeat, the future feeling fixed and small, as though the next twenty years would look much like the last few. What kept him moving forward was the quiet accumulation of these moments and the realization that his body was still waiting for a threat that had already passed. At forty-two, with a PCL-5 score that finally pushed him to book an appointment, Sione sat in the waiting room listening to the reception door click open. He was afraid he would spend his life braced for the next grab, but he also hoped, for the first time, that he might be able to step out of the late afternoon shadows and remember the whole picture.
